claims.claim: Ubiquitination of the mitofusins is one of the very first steps after the induction of mitophagy.
claims.source: Thus, ubiquitination of the mitofusins is one of the very first steps after the induction of mitophagy.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the rapid ubiquitination kinetics of Mfn1 and Mfn2 compared to other OMM proteins

claims.claim: Robust coimmunoprecipitation of ubiquitinated Mfn1 and Mfn2 with GFP-parkinWT occurs at one hour CCCP.
claims.source: We observed robust coimmunoprecipitation of ubiquitinated Mfn1 and Mfn2 with GFP-parkinWT at one hour CCCP (corresponding to the Ub burst observed in Figure 2B), with no apparent binding at four hours (Figure 2C), likely due to turnover of the Mfns by the proteasome at this time (Figures 1G and 2B and [Tanaka et al., 2010]).
claims.evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C

claims.claim: Ubiquitinated Miro1 binds to WT parkin only at four hours of CCCP treatment.
claims.source: When we analyzed other parkin substrates that are ubiquitinated less rapidly than the Mfns (Figure 2A), we observed binding to WT parkin only at four hours of CCCP treatment in the case of ubiquitinated Miro1, and binding of mono-ubiquitinated HK1 at one hour CCCP, which was further shifted at four hours, indicative of processivity of HK1 ubiquitination (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C

claims.claim: Mono-ubiquitinated HK1 binds to WT parkin at one hour CCCP, which is further shifted at four hours, indicative of processivity of HK1 ubiquitination.
claims.source: When we analyzed other parkin substrates that are ubiquitinated less rapidly than the Mfns (Figure 2A), we observed binding to WT parkin only at four hours of CCCP treatment in the case of ubiquitinated Miro1, and binding of mono-ubiquitinated HK1 at one hour CCCP, which was further shifted at four hours, indicative of processivity of HK1 ubiquitination (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C

claims.claim: None of the ubiquitinated species coimmunoprecipitated with GFP-parkinA320R.
claims.source: None of these ubiquitinated species coimmunoprecipitated with GFP-parkinA320R (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C

claims.claim: GFP-parkin binds ubiquitinated Mfn2.
claims.source: To confirm that GFP-parkin was indeed binding ubiquitinated Mfn2, we treated GFP-parkin immunoprecipitates from CCCP-treated cells with Usp2 deubiquitinase (see schematic in Figure 2D), which is active on both phosphorylated and unphosphorylated Ub chains (Wauer et al., 2015b), and observed the release of Mfn2 from the parkin-bound bead fraction into the supernatant after separation by centrifugation (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: Supported by on-bead deubiquitination data shown in Figure 2E

claims.claim: Early on in the mitophagy pathway, parkin binds ubiquitinated Mfn2, likely through interactions with pUb moieties.
claims.source: These results strongly suggested that, early on in the mitophagy pathway, parkin was binding ubiquitinated Mfn2, likely through interactions with pUb moieties.
claims.evidence: Inferred from coimmunoprecipitation and deubiquitination experiments

claims.claim: Mfn2 immunoprecipitation from CCCP-treated U2OS:GFP-parkinWT cells contains Ub-modified species.
claims.source: When we immunoprecipitated Mfn2 from U2OS:GFP-parkinWT cells that were treated with CCCP for one hour, we detected Ub-modified species by immunoblot (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2F

claims.claim: LC/MS confirmed that the Mfn2 immunoprecipitation contained pS65 Ub selectively in the CCCP-treated condition.
claims.source: Liquid-chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry (LC/MS) confirmed that the Mfn2 immunoprecipitation contained pS65 Ub selectively in the CCCP-treated condition (Figure 2G), despite lower Mfn2 levels (Figure 2A and F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by LC/MS data shown in Figure 2G

claims.claim: Both pS65 and unphosphorylated Ub are covalently attached to Mfn2.
claims.source: We then confirmed that both pS65 and unphosphorylated Ub were covalently attached to Mfn2 by its precipitation under denaturing conditions and detecting pS65 Ub and total Ub by immunoblot (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: Supported by denaturing immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2H

claims.claim: pS65 Ub, Ub and (shifted) Mfn2 can be detected in GST-R0RBRWT pulldowns in a CCCP-dependent manner.
claims.source: In a CCCP-dependent manner, pS65 Ub, Ub and (shifted) Mfn2 could be detected in GST-R0RBRWT pulldowns (Figure 2J).
claims.evidence: Supported by GST pulldown data shown in Figure 2J

claims.claim: pS65 Ub, Ub and Mfn2 are not observed in pulldowns using GST-R0RBRA320R.
claims.source: Strikingly, we did not observe any of these factors in pulldowns using GST-R0RBRA320R (Figure 2J).
claims.evidence: Supported by GST pulldown data shown in Figure 2J

claims.claim: Mfn2 is phosphoubiquitinated during mitochondrial depolarization.
claims.source: Mfn2 is therefore phosphoubiquitinated and, taken together with our previous data, a burst of phosphoubiquitination – parkin-mediated ubiquitination coupled to PINK1-catalyzed phosphorylation – occurs on Mfn2 at an early time point in the mitophagy pathway.
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple experiments including LC/MS, denaturing IP, and GST pulldowns

claims.claim: A burst of phosphoubiquitination occurs on Mfn2 at an early time point in the mitophagy pathway.
claims.source: Mfn2 is therefore phosphoubiquitinated and, taken together with our previous data, a burst of phosphoubiquitination – parkin-mediated ubiquitination coupled to PINK1-catalyzed phosphorylation – occurs on Mfn2 at an early time point in the mitophagy pathway.
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple experiments showing rapid Mfn2 ubiquitination and phosphoubiquitination

claims.claim: Mfn2 silencing increases mitochondrial fragmentation in U2OS:GFP-parkinWT cells.
claims.source: We confirmed Mfn1 and Mfn2 depletion by immunoblot (Figure 3A), and observed mitochondrial fragmentation in both siMfn1 and siMfn2 cells (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B) with an ER-OMM apposition defect unique to the siMfn2 condition (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C and D), as expected.
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B

claims.claim: Mfn2 silencing causes an ER-OMM apposition defect.
claims.source: We confirmed Mfn1 and Mfn2 depletion by immunoblot (Figure 3A), and observed mitochondrial fragmentation in both siMfn1 and siMfn2 cells (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B) with an ER-OMM apposition defect unique to the siMfn2 condition (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C and D), as expected.
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, C and D

claims.claim: Mfn2 silencing increases the kinetics of parkin recruitment to depolarized mitochondria.
claims.source: Remarkably, we observed faster mitochondrial recruitment in siMfn2 (but not siMfn1) cells, under both bioenergetic conditions (Figure 3C and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by parkin recruitment data shown in Figure 3C and D

claims.claim: Mfn2 silencing increases parkin recruitment in galactose-grown cells to levels seen in glucose-maintained cells transfected with control siRNA.
claims.source: Strikingly, Mfn2 silencing increased recruitment in galactose-grown cells to levels seen in glucose-maintained cells transfected with control siRNA (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: Supported by parkin recruitment data shown in Figure 3E

claims.claim: Silencing Mfn1 and Mfn2 simultaneously does not further enhance the kinetics of parkin recruitment beyond single, Mfn2-depleted cells.
claims.source: Silencing Mfn1 and Mfn2 simultaneously (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) did not further enhance the kinetics of parkin recruitment beyond single, Mfn2-depleted cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D), implying that this phenotype was Mfn2-specific and unrelated to a loss of mitochondrial fusion.
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-D

claims.claim: The increased parkin recruitment phenotype in Mfn2-depleted cells is Mfn2-specific and unrelated to a loss of mitochondrial fusion.
claims.source: Silencing Mfn1 and Mfn2 simultaneously (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) did not further enhance the kinetics of parkin recruitment beyond single, Mfn2-depleted cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D), implying that this phenotype was Mfn2-specific and unrelated to a loss of mitochondrial fusion.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that double knockdown does not enhance the phenotype beyond Mfn2 single knockdown

claims.claim: Silencing of PACS2 or Stx17 increases the translocation of parkin to mitochondria.
claims.source: When we tested parkin recruitment in these cells, we saw that, similarly to Mfn2 knockdown, silencing of either PACS2 (siPACS2) or Stx17 (siStx17) increased the translocation of parkin to mitochondria (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G and H).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3G and H

claims.claim: Disruption of mitochondrion-ER tethering increases the kinetics of parkin translocation to depolarized mitochondria.
claims.source: Thus, disruption of mitochondrion-ER tethering increases the kinetics of parkin translocation to depolarized mitochondria.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experiments showing increased parkin recruitment upon silencing of Mfn2, PACS2, and Stx17

claims.claim: In Mfn2-depleted cells, depolarization-induced mitophagy is enhanced.
claims.source: These data demonstrate that, in Mfn2-depleted cells, depolarization-induced mitophagy is enhanced, in line with our parkin recruitment experiments (Figure 3A to E), and demonstrate that Mfn2 represses mitophagy at the level of pathway initiation.
claims.evidence: Supported by mtKeima data shown in Figure 3F and G

claims.claim: Mfn2 represses mitophagy at the level of pathway initiation.
claims.source: These data demonstrate that, in Mfn2-depleted cells, depolarization-induced mitophagy is enhanced, in line with our parkin recruitment experiments (Figure 3A to E), and demonstrate that Mfn2 represses mitophagy at the level of pathway initiation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from enhanced mitophagy and faster parkin recruitment in Mfn2-depleted cells

claims.claim: Mfn2 KO cells display increased recruitment kinetics of GFP-parkin.
claims.source: Corroborating our earlier data in siMfn2 cells, Mfn2 KO cells (grown on glucose) transiently transfected with GFP-parkin displayed increased recruitment kinetics (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E and F) and increased mitophagy (Figure 3—figure supplement 4G and H).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4E and F

claims.claim: Mfn2 KO cells display increased mitophagy.
claims.source: Corroborating our earlier data in siMfn2 cells, Mfn2 KO cells (grown on glucose) transiently transfected with GFP-parkin displayed increased recruitment kinetics (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E and F) and increased mitophagy (Figure 3—figure supplement 4G and H).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4G and H

claims.claim: Parkin translocation in Mfn2 KO cells remains PINK1-dependent.
claims.source: Finally, we ensured that parkin translocation in Mfn2 KO cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A–C) and U2OS:GFP-parkin cells depleted of Mfn2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 5D) remained PINK1-dependent.
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A-D

claims.claim: Cells expressing GFP-parkinA320R fail to translocate under conditions of Mfn2-depletion.
claims.source: Moreover, cells expressing GFP-parkinA320R (Figure 3—figure supplement 5E) failed to translocate under conditions of Mfn2-depletion (Figure 3—figure supplement 5F and G).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5F and G

claims.claim: Mfn2 reduction increases on-pathway mitophagy kinetics.
claims.source: This indicates a clear requirement for PINK1 and Ub phosphorylation for parkin translocation in Mfn2-depleted cells, demonstrating that Mfn2 reduction increases on-pathway mitophagy kinetics.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the requirement for PINK1 and pUb-binding for parkin translocation in Mfn2-depleted cells

claims.claim: Mitochondria-ER contact is dispensable for mitophagy.
claims.source: Taken together, our data not only show that mitochondria-ER contact is dispensable for mitophagy, but that this type of organellar coupling in fact antagonizes the pathway.
claims.evidence: Inferred from data showing enhanced mitophagy upon disruption of mitochondria-ER contacts

claims.claim: Mitochondria-ER tethering antagonizes mitophagy.
claims.source: Taken together, our data not only show that mitochondria-ER contact is dispensable for mitophagy, but that this type of organellar coupling in fact antagonizes the pathway.
claims.evidence: Inferred from data showing enhanced mitophagy upon disruption of mitochondria-ER contacts

claims.claim: Ectopic expression of Mfn2, but not Mfn1, suppresses the recruitment of YFP-parkin to depolarized mitochondria in Mfn2 KO cells.
claims.source: Turning to recruitment assays – in which we observed faster GFP-parkin recruitment in Mfn2 KO cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E and F) – we observed that ectopic expression of Mfn2, but not Mfn1, was able to suppress the recruitment of YFP-parkin to depolarized mitochondria (Figure 4B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B and C

claims.claim: The antagonistic effect of Mfn2 on mitophagy occurs through its ability to tether mitochondria to the ER and not its effect on mitochondrial fusion.
claims.source: This is in line with our previous data showing that the antagonistic effect of Mfn2 on mitophagy occurs through its ability to tether mitochondria to the ER (Figure 3—figure supplement 3H–J) and not its effect on mitochondrial fusion (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-D and 3H-J

claims.claim: Mutation of K406, K416 and K420 in the HR1 domain (Mfn2HR1) reduces CCCP-induced ubiquitination of Mfn2 by ~75%.
claims.source: We thus posited that mutation of several lysine residues would likely be required to reduce Mfn2 ubiquitination. While mutation of all major sites of Mfn2 ubiquitination almost completely abolishes its modification by parkin (Heo et al., 2015), we found that mutation of K406, K416 and K420 in the HR1 domain (Mfn2HR1) reduced its CCCP-induced ubiquitination by ~75%, as measured by the disappearance of the unmodified band by immunoblot (Figure 4E and F; here Mfn2 levels are normalized to the untreated condition for each construct).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E and F

claims.claim: Mutation of all four sites in HR2 (Mfn2HR2) fails to significantly reduce Mfn2 modification.
claims.source: This effect was greater than what we observed with the single mutant, Mfn2K406R (K416 and K420 appear dispensable in this assay), and mutation of all four sites in HR2 (Mfn2HR2) or the double T111A/S442A phosphomutant (Mfn2TS/AA) failed to significantly reduce Mfn2 modification (Figure 4E and F).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E and F

claims.claim: The double T111A/S442A phosphomutant (Mfn2TS/AA) fails to significantly reduce Mfn2 modification.
claims.source: This effect was greater than what we observed with the single mutant, Mfn2K406R (K416 and K420 appear dispensable in this assay), and mutation of all four sites in HR2 (Mfn2HR2) or the double T111A/S442A phosphomutant (Mfn2TS/AA) failed to significantly reduce Mfn2 modification (Figure 4E and F).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E and F

claims.claim: Mfn2HR1, Mfn2HR2 and Mfn2T111A/S442A rescue mitochondrial morphology in a similar manner to WT Mfn2.
claims.source: Introduction of either Mfn2HR1, Mfn2HR2 or Mfn2T111A/S442A into Mfn2 KO:YFP-parkin cells rescued morphology in a similar manner to WT Mfn2 (Figure 4H), demonstrating these mutations did not disrupt mitochondrial fusion.
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4H

claims.claim: All three Mfn2 mutants (HR1, HR2 and T111A/S442A) form HMW complexes similar to WT.
claims.source: By blue native polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (BN-PAGE), we observed that all three mutants (HR1, HR2 and T111A/S442A) formed HMW complexes similar to WT in solubilized mitochondria (Figure 4I).
claims.evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 4I

claims.claim: Only rescue of Mfn2 with Mfn2HR1 blocks the turnover of mitochondria in Mfn2 KO:YFP-parkinWT cells.
claims.source: When we assayed mitophagy in Mfn2 KO:YFP-parkinWT cells, we found that only rescue of Mfn2 with Mfn2HR1 – the ubiquitination of which is compromised (Figure 4E and F) – blocked the turnover of mitochondria (Figure 4J and K).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4J and K

claims.claim: Ubiquitination of the Mfn2 HR1 domain by parkin is required for efficient mitophagy.
claims.source: Thus, ubiquitination of the Mfn2 HR1 domain by parkin is required for efficient mitophagy and, taken together with our previous mitophagic data in Mfn2-depleted cells, demonstrates that parkin and PINK1 directly counter Mfn2-mediated mitochondria-ER tethering through Mfn2 turnover to promote mitophagy.
claims.evidence: Inferred from data showing that Mfn2HR1 blocks mitophagy

claims.claim: Parkin and PINK1 directly counter Mfn2-mediated mitochondria-ER tethering through Mfn2 turnover to promote mitophagy.
claims.source: Thus, ubiquitination of the Mfn2 HR1 domain by parkin is required for efficient mitophagy and, taken together with our previous mitophagic data in Mfn2-depleted cells, demonstrates that parkin and PINK1 directly counter Mfn2-mediated mitochondria-ER tethering through Mfn2 turnover to promote mitophagy.
claims.evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing Mfn2 ubiquitination, turnover, and effects on mitophagy

claims.claim: Mfn2 exists in a bimodal distribution into two complexes, weighing approximately ~250 kDa and ~500 kDa.
claims.source: Examining HMW complexes by BN-PAGE in untreated U2OS:GFP-parkinWT cells (expressing endogenous Mfn2), we observed a bimodal distribution of Mfn2 into two complexes, weighing approximately ~250 kDa and ~500 kDa (Figure 5A, leftmost lane, similar to what was seen in Figure 4I).
claims.evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 5A

claims.claim: Mfn1 only forms a ~ 250 kDa HMW complex.
claims.source: By contrast, Mfn1 – which, in our assays, appears dispensable for mitochondria-ER tethering as assayed by EM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and its effect on parkin recruitment (Figure 3C–E) – only formed a ~ 250 kDa HMW complex (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 5A

claims.claim: The ~500 kDa complex containing solely Mfn2 is a dimer of the ~250 kDa Mfn2-containing subcomplex that potentially bridges the ER and OMM.
claims.source: We thus considered the ~500 kDa complex containing solely Mfn2 as a dimer of the ~250 kDa Mfn2-containing subcomplex that potentially bridges the ER and OMM.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that Mfn2 uniquely forms a ~500 kDa complex and its known role in ER-OMM tethering

claims.claim: CCCP treatment causes a rapid loss of Mfn2- (and Mfn1-) containing HMW complexes.
claims.source: Upon CCCP treatment, we observed a rapid loss Mfn2- (and Mfn1-) containing complexes (Figure 5A), concomitant with its phosphoubiquitination (Figure 2) and dependent upon parkin ligase activity (Figure 5B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 5A, B, and C

claims.claim: The disappearance of HMW Mfn complexes is predominantly due to their extraction from the OMM.
claims.source: While treatment of mitochondrial lysates with Usp2 deubiquitinase slightly increased levels of the unmodified Mfn1 or Mfn2 band in mitochondria isolated from CCCP-treated cells (Figure 5D; the densitometry measurements correspond to the shorter exposures of Mfn1 and Mfn2), this was not to levels seen in mitochondria from untreated cells. This result indicated that the disappearance of HMW Mfn complexes are predominantly due to their extraction from the OMM (and not a high level of modification by Ub).
claims.evidence: Supported by Usp2 treatment data shown in Figure 5D

claims.claim: Extraction of HMW Mfn complexes is mediated by the AAA-ATPase p97/VCP.
claims.source: This process is thought to be mediated by the AAA-ATPase p97/VCP (Tanaka et al., 2010) and, accordingly, when we treated U2OS:GFP-parkinWT cells with CCCP in the presence of the non-competitive p97 inhibitor NMS-873 (Magnaghi et al., 2013), extraction of HMW complexes containing either Mfn1 or Mfn2 was accordingly repressed (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Tanaka et al., 2010 and data shown in Figure 5E

claims.claim: Both ~250 kDa (containing Mfn1 and/or Mfn2) and ~500 kDa (Mfn2 only) complexes are stabilized in the presence of NMS-873.
claims.source: Indeed, both ~250 kDa (containing Mfn1 and/or Mfn2) and ~500 kDa (Mfn2 only) complexes were stabilized in the presence of NMS-873 (Figure 5E), with smearing occurring due to Mfn ubiquitination (see Figure 2), indicating that parkin-mediated ubiquitination itself was not sufficient to drive apart the ~500 kDa Mfn2-containing interorganellar bridge.
claims.evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 5E

claims.claim: Parkin-mediated ubiquitination itself is not sufficient to drive apart the ~500 kDa Mfn2-containing interorganellar bridge.
claims.source: Indeed, both ~250 kDa (containing Mfn1 and/or Mfn2) and ~500 kDa (Mfn2 only) complexes were stabilized in the presence of NMS-873 (Figure 5E), with smearing occurring due to Mfn ubiquitination (see Figure 2), indicating that parkin-mediated ubiquitination itself was not sufficient to drive apart the ~500 kDa Mfn2-containing interorganellar bridge.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that ubiquitinated Mfn2 complexes remain intact when p97 is inhibited

claims.claim: p97 inhibition prevents the dissociation of mitochondria from the ER during mitophagy.
claims.source: Analysis of OMM-ER appositions in these cells revealed that p97 inhibition prevented the dissociation of mitochondria from the ER (Figure 5F–H).
claims.evidence: Supported by EM data shown in Figure 5F-H

claims.claim: p97-dependent extraction of Mfn2 HMW complexes from the OMM separates mitochondria from the ER during mitophagy.
claims.source: Thus, p97-dependent extraction of Mfn2 HMW complexes from the OMM separates mitochondria from the ER during mitophagy.
claims.evidence: Inferred from data showing that p97 inhibition prevents both Mfn2 complex extraction and ER-OMM dissociation

claims.claim: NMS-873 co-incubation completely blocks the mitochondrial translocation of p97 in CCCP-treated cells.
claims.source: Consistent with our HMW complex extraction data (Figure 5E), co-incubation of cells with CCCP and NMS-873 completely blocked the mitochondrial translocation of p97 (Figure 6A and B) which occurs during mitophagy (Kimura et al., 2013; Tanaka et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6A and B and citations to Kimura et al., 2013; Tanaka et al., 2010

claims.claim: p97 depletion increases ubiquitinated Mfn2 upon depolarization.
claims.source: We observed a similar effect when we silenced p97 with siRNA (sip97); in p97-depleted cells treated with CCCP, we saw an increase in ubiquitinated Mfn2 upon depolarization (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6E

claims.claim: Basal levels of Mfn2 increase upon prolonged p97 depletion.
claims.source: Additionally, basal levels of Mfn2 increased upon prolonged p97 depletion (Figure 6E), consistent with the possible involvement of p97 in steady-state Mfn2 turnover (Zhang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6E and citation to Zhang et al., 2017

claims.claim: NMS-873 stabilizes ubiquitinated Mfn2 in Mfn2 KO:YFP-parkinWT cells rescued with WT Mfn2.
claims.source: In Mfn2 KO:YFP-parkinWT cells rescued with WT Mfn2, CCCP induced Mfn2 turnover and, when cells were co-incubated with NMS-873, we observed a stabilization of ubiquitinated Mfn2 (Figure 6F) similar to WT U2OS cells expressing GFP-parkin (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6F

claims.claim: Mfn2HR1 shows a severe reduction in NMS-873-dependent stabilization of CCCP-induced Mfn2-Ub conjugates.
claims.source: When we expressed Mfn2HR1 in Mfn2 KO:YFP-parkinWT cells, we observed a severe reduction in NMS-873-dependent stabilization of CCCP-induced Mfn2-Ub conjugates (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6F

claims.claim: Ubiquitination of lysines in the Mfn2 HR1 domain is recognized by p97 and signals for extraction of the protein.
claims.source: We confirmed this reduction in ubiquitination by immunoprecipiting Mfn2 from reconstituted cells treated with CCCP and NMS-873 under denaturing conditions and immunoblotting for Ub (Figure 6G). This supports our mutagenesis data showing a reduction of Mfn2HR1 turnover (Figure 4E and F) and is mechanistically consistent with ubiquitination of lysines in the Mfn2 HR1 domain being recognized by p97 and signaling for extraction of the protein.
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6G and inferred from mutagenesis data

claims.claim: Ubiquitinated Mfn2 is not the sole p97-binding protein on the OMM.
claims.source: While we posited that Mfn2 may be acting as a p97 receptor during mitophagy, we observed robust p97 recruitment in depolarized Mfn2 KO:YFP-parkinWT cells (Figure 6H and I). Moreover, p97 recruitment was similar in cells expressing either Mfn2WT or Mfn2HR1 (Figure 6H and I). p97 recruitment levels in both Mfn2 rescue conditions were lower than in cells transfected with empty vector (Figure 6H and I) likely owing to the delayed parkin recruitment kinetics in Mfn2-expressing cells (Figure 4B and C). Thus, ubiquitinated Mfn2 is not the sole p97-binding protein on the OMM.
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6H and I

claims.claim: The interaction between parkin and ubiquitinated Mfn2 is stabilized when cells are co-treated with CCCP and NMS-873.
claims.source: As we detected pUb conjugated to immunoprecipitated Mfn2 from cells treated with CCCP (Figure 2G and H), we co-treated cells with CCCP and NMS-873 and observed that the interaction between parkin and ubiquitinated Mfn2 – which is normally transient owing to Mfn2 turnover – was stabilized (Figure 6J and K).
claims.evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6J and K

claims.claim: p97, as well as its cofactors p47 and UBXN1, are present in 4xUb pull-downs and almost totally absent in parallel 4xpUb pull-downs.
claims.source: Using nearly fully-phosphorylated chains (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), we consistently observed the presence of p97, as well as its cofactors p47 and UBXN1, in 4xUb pull-downs, and these proteins were almost totally absent in parallel 4xpUb pull-downs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by LC/MS data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claims.claim: While p97 mediates the turnover of ubiquitinated Mfn2, this likely does not involve interactions between the p97 complex and pUb.
claims.source: Thus, while p97 mediates the turnover of ubiquitinated Mfn2, this likely does not involve interactions between the p97 complex and pUb.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that p97 binds unphosphorylated Ub chains but not phosphorylated Ub chains

claims.claim: Parkin-mediated ubiquitination on its own is insufficient to drive the disassembly of Mfn2 HMW complexes in the absence of p97 activity.
claims.source: The herein-described role of p97 in separating mitochondria from the ER is critical; parkin-mediated ubiquitination on its own appears to be insufficient to drive the disassembly of Mfn2 HMW complexes (Figure 5E) or to dissociate the ER from the OMM (Figure 5F and G) in the absence of p97 activity.
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E, F, and G

claims.claim: In the absence of Mfn2, inhibition of p97 fails to suppress mitophagy.
claims.source: When cells were depleted of Mfn2 (siMfn2), p97 inhibition reduced the rate of mtKeima acidification (Figure 7A and B, dark and light blue bars), but mitophagy was still permissive. Indeed, the number of cells with acidified mtKeima in siMfn2 cells treated with NMS-873 was still ~5 fold greater than their DMSO treated counterparts (Figure 7B, light blue bar), which was more of an increase that was observed for control cells with active p97 (Figure 7B, red bar). Thus, in the absence of Mfn2, inhibition of p97 fails to suppress mitophagy, demonstrating that a significant component of the role of p97 in mitophagy functions through Mfn2.
claims.evidence: Supported by mtKeima data shown in Figure 7A and B

claims.claim: A significant component of the role of p97 in mitophagy functions through Mfn2.
claims.source: Thus, in the absence of Mfn2, inhibition of p97 fails to suppress mitophagy, demonstrating that a significant component of the role of p97 in mitophagy functions through Mfn2.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that p97 inhibition does not block mitophagy in Mfn2-depleted cells

claims.claim: The parkin-dependent ubiquitination of VDAC1 is sensitive to p97 inhibition in control cells, but not cells depleted of Mfn2.
claims.source: We observed that the parkin-dependent ubiquitination of VDAC1 – which has been reported to form a complex with pUb and parkin that is stable over a period of hours (Callegari et al., 2017) – was sensitive to p97 inhibition in control cells, but not cells depleted of Mfn2 (Figure 7C–E).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7C-E and citation to Callegari et al., 2017

claims.claim: The half-time of VDAC1 modification during mitophagy increases two-fold in the presence of NMS-873 specifically in control cells compared to cells transfected with siMfn2.
claims.source: Indeed, the half-time of VDAC1 modification during mitophagy increased two-fold in the presence of NMS-873 specifically in control cells compared to cells transfected with siMfn2 (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7F

claims.claim: Cells depleted of Mfn1 are comparable to control siRNA-transfected cells with respect to the effect of NMS-873 on VDAC1 modification.
claims.source: Notably, cells depleted of Mfn1 were comparable to control siRNA-transfected cells in this regard (Figure 7G and H).

results.result: Loss of PRKN or PINK1 causes early-onset hereditary Parkinson's disease, which is linked to mitochondrial dysfunction.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 are well-established facts in the field, supported by multiple citations (Kitada et al., 1998; Ryan et al., 2015; Valente et al., 2004). These are background claims establishing the disease context for the study.

results.result: PINK1 and parkin promote mitochondrial health through multiple quality control mechanisms including proteasomal degradation, mitochondrial-derived vesicles, and mitophagy, where PINK1 activates parkin through phosphorylation and phosphoubiquitin generation, leading to ubiquitination of OMM proteins and recruitment of autophagic machinery.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C12 describe well-established mechanisms of PINK1/parkin-mediated mitochondrial quality control, supported by multiple citations. These are background claims providing context for the current study's findings.

results.result: Mitochondria-ER contact sites are required for starvation-induced autophagosome formation, and Mfn2 acts as a mitochondria-ER tether required for this process, yet is also ubiquitinated and degraded by parkin, creating an apparent conflict with the assumption that parkin-dependent mitophagy follows a similar mechanism to yeast mitophagy.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C20 establish the scientific context and paradox that motivates the study. These are well-supported by citations and identify the key question: how can Mfn2 be both required for autophagosome formation and degraded during mitophagy?

results.result: Parkin disrupts mitochondria-ER contacts during mitophagy as an early step before autophagosomal engulfment, reducing both the percentage of OMM in contact with ER and the percentage of mitochondria connected to ER in depolarized cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C28 are supported by quantitative EM data (Figure 1A-E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing robust reduction in ER-OMM contacts across multiple distance thresholds (100, 50, 25 nm) in CCCP-treated GFP-parkin expressing cells. The effect is specific to parkin and occurs before autophagosomal engulfment.

results.result: The destruction of mitochondria-ER contacts during mitophagy requires parkin, PINK1, and proteasomal activity, as demonstrated by rescue of ER-OMM contacts with MG132 proteasome inhibition or PINK1 depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C29, C30, and C33 are supported by EM data (Figure 1H-J) showing that both proteasome inhibition (MG132) and PINK1 depletion prevent ER-OMM disruption in CCCP-treated cells. This establishes the mechanistic requirements for contact site destruction.

results.result: Mitochondria-ER contacts are destroyed during mitophagy in both heterologous cell cultures and dopaminergic neurons, with CCCP inducing Mfn2 ubiquitination and decreased ER-OMM appositions in control but not parkin-deletion iDA neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C31, C32, and C121 are supported by data from both U2OS cells and iDA neurons (Figure 1M-O). The observation in dopaminergic neurons is particularly important given the relevance to Parkinson's disease. The parkin-dependence is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Mfn1 and Mfn2 undergo rapid ubiquitination within the first 30-60 minutes of CCCP treatment, much faster than other OMM proteins like TOM20, making mitofusin ubiquitination one of the earliest steps in mitophagy.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C38 are supported by time-course immunoblot data (Figure 2A-B) showing rapid Mfn turnover and ubiquitination burst between 30-60 min, contrasting with gradual TOM20 ubiquitination over hours. This establishes temporal hierarchy of substrate ubiquitination.

results.result: Parkin binds ubiquitinated Mfn2 early in mitophagy (1 hour CCCP) through pUb interactions, as demonstrated by coimmunoprecipitation and deubiquitination experiments, with different temporal patterns for other substrates like Miro1 and HK1.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C44 are supported by coimmunoprecipitation data (Figure 2C) and on-bead deubiquitination (Figure 2E). The A320R mutant controls demonstrate pUb-dependence. The temporal hierarchy of substrate binding is clearly established.

results.result: Mfn2 is phosphoubiquitinated during mitochondrial depolarization, with a burst of phosphoubiquitination occurring early in mitophagy, as demonstrated by LC/MS detection of pS65 Ub, denaturing IP, and GST-R0RBR pulldowns.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C51 are supported by multiple complementary approaches (Figure 2F-J): LC/MS showing pS65 Ub (Figure 2G), denaturing IP confirming covalent attachment (Figure 2H), and GST-R0RBR pulldowns showing A320R-sensitive binding. This provides strong evidence for Mfn2 phosphoubiquitination.

results.result: Mfn2 silencing increases mitochondrial fragmentation and causes an ER-OMM apposition defect, while specifically increasing the kinetics of parkin recruitment to depolarized mitochondria in both glucose and galactose conditions, with this phenotype being Mfn2-specific and unrelated to loss of mitochondrial fusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C57 are supported by multiple experiments (Figure 3A-E, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-D) showing that Mfn2 but not Mfn1 depletion accelerates parkin recruitment, and double knockdown doesn't enhance the effect beyond Mfn2 alone. This demonstrates Mfn2-specific regulation of mitophagy initiation.

results.result: Disruption of mitochondrion-ER tethering by silencing PACS2 or Stx17 increases the kinetics of parkin translocation to depolarized mitochondria, similar to Mfn2 knockdown.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 are supported by parkin recruitment data (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G-H) showing that silencing other ER-OMM tethering proteins produces similar effects to Mfn2 depletion. This generalizes the finding beyond Mfn2 to ER-OMM tethering per se.

results.result: Mfn2 represses mitophagy at the level of pathway initiation, as demonstrated by enhanced depolarization-induced mitophagy in Mfn2-depleted cells and Mfn2 KO cells, with increased recruitment kinetics and increased mitochondrial turnover.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 are supported by mtKeima flow cytometry data (Figure 3F-G) and additional experiments in Mfn2 KO cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E-H). The data show enhanced mitophagy in Mfn2-depleted conditions, consistent with Mfn2 acting as a negative regulator.

results.result: Parkin translocation in Mfn2-depleted cells remains PINK1-dependent and requires pUb-binding, as cells expressing GFP-parkinA320R fail to translocate under Mfn2-depletion conditions, demonstrating that Mfn2 reduction increases on-pathway mitophagy kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by data (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A-G) showing PINK1 requirement and A320R mutant failure to translocate in Mfn2-depleted cells. This confirms that enhanced mitophagy in Mfn2-depleted cells operates through the canonical PINK1/parkin pathway.

results.result: Mitochondria-ER contacts are not only dispensable for mitophagy but actively antagonize the pathway, as their reduction facilitates parkin substrate ubiquitination, parkin translocation, and mitochondrial turnover.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 and C123-C124 represent a major conclusion supported by multiple lines of evidence showing enhanced mitophagy upon disruption of ER-OMM contacts. This fundamentally challenges the assumption that mitophagy requires ER-mitochondria contacts like starvation-induced autophagy.

results.result: Ectopic expression of Mfn2, but not Mfn1, suppresses parkin recruitment to depolarized mitochondria in Mfn2 KO cells, with this antagonistic effect occurring through Mfn2's ability to tether mitochondria to the ER rather than its effect on mitochondrial fusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 are supported by rescue experiments (Figure 4B-C) and prior data distinguishing tethering from fusion functions. This demonstrates that Mfn2's specific role in ER-OMM tethering, not fusion, mediates its inhibitory effect on mitophagy.

results.result: Mutation of K406, K416, and K420 in the HR1 domain (Mfn2HR1) reduces CCCP-induced ubiquitination by ~75%, while HR2 and phosphomutant mutations do not significantly reduce modification, and all mutants rescue mitochondrial morphology and form HMW complexes similar to WT.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 are supported by mutagenesis data (Figure 4E-I) showing differential effects of mutations on ubiquitination while preserving fusion function and complex formation. This identifies specific lysines in HR1 as critical ubiquitination sites.

results.result: Ubiquitination of the Mfn2 HR1 domain by parkin is required for efficient mitophagy, as only rescue with Mfn2HR1 blocks mitochondrial turnover, demonstrating that parkin and PINK1 directly counter Mfn2-mediated mitochondria-ER tethering through Mfn2 turnover to promote mitophagy.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 are supported by mitophagy assays (Figure 4J-K) showing that Mfn2HR1 blocks mitophagy while other mutants do not. This establishes the functional importance of HR1 ubiquitination and provides mechanistic insight into how parkin promotes mitophagy.

results.result: Mfn2 exists in a bimodal distribution of ~250 kDa and ~500 kDa complexes, while Mfn1 only forms ~250 kDa complexes, with the ~500 kDa Mfn2 complex potentially representing a dimer bridging ER and OMM that is rapidly lost upon CCCP treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 are supported by BN-PAGE data (Figure 5A) showing distinct complex patterns for Mfn1 and Mfn2. The interpretation of the ~500 kDa complex as an interorganellar bridge is reasonable but somewhat speculative (C81 includes speculation).

results.result: The disappearance of HMW Mfn complexes is predominantly due to p97-mediated extraction from the OMM rather than high-level ubiquitination, as p97 inhibition with NMS-873 stabilizes both ~250 kDa and ~500 kDa complexes, indicating that ubiquitination alone is insufficient to disassemble the Mfn2 interorganellar bridge.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 are supported by Usp2 treatment (Figure 5D) and p97 inhibitor experiments (Figure 5E). The data clearly show that p97 activity is required for complex disassembly beyond ubiquitination alone, establishing p97's critical role.

results.result: p97 inhibition prevents the dissociation of mitochondria from the ER during mitophagy, demonstrating that p97-dependent extraction of Mfn2 HMW complexes from the OMM separates mitochondria from the ER.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 are supported by EM data (Figure 5F-H) showing that NMS-873 prevents ER-OMM dissociation. This directly links p97 activity to the physical separation of organelles, completing the mechanistic picture.

results.result: p97 inhibition with NMS-873 blocks mitochondrial translocation of p97 and stabilizes ubiquitinated Mfn2, with p97 depletion increasing ubiquitinated Mfn2 and basal Mfn2 levels, consistent with p97 involvement in both mitophagy and steady-state Mfn2 turnover.
results.evaluation: Claims C89, C91-C92 are supported by p97 translocation data (Figure 6A-B), p97 inhibition/depletion experiments (Figure 6C-E), and citation to Zhang et al., 2017. This establishes p97's role in Mfn2 turnover during mitophagy.

results.result: NMS-873 stabilizes ubiquitinated Mfn2 in cells rescued with WT Mfn2 but not Mfn2HR1, demonstrating that ubiquitination of lysines in the Mfn2 HR1 domain is recognized by p97 and signals for protein extraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 are supported by experiments in reconstituted Mfn2 KO cells (Figure 6F-G) showing differential stabilization of WT vs HR1 mutant. This links the HR1 ubiquitination sites to p97 recognition and extraction.

results.result: Ubiquitinated Mfn2 is not the sole p97-binding protein on the OMM, as robust p97 recruitment occurs in Mfn2 KO cells and is similar in cells expressing Mfn2WT or Mfn2HR1.
results.evaluation: Claim C96 is supported by p97 recruitment data (Figure 6H-I) showing that p97 recruitment occurs independently of Mfn2. This indicates that p97 has multiple substrates on the OMM during mitophagy.

results.result: The interaction between parkin and ubiquitinated Mfn2 is stabilized when p97 is inhibited, and p97 binds unphosphorylated but not phosphorylated Ub chains, indicating that p97-mediated Mfn2 turnover likely does not involve p97-pUb interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 are supported by coimmunoprecipitation (Figure 6J-K) and LC/MS pulldown data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C). The finding that p97 preferentially binds unphosphorylated Ub is important for understanding the mechanism.

results.result: Parkin-mediated ubiquitination alone is insufficient to drive Mfn2 HMW complex disassembly or ER-OMM dissociation without p97 activity, and in the absence of Mfn2, p97 inhibition fails to suppress mitophagy, demonstrating that a significant component of p97's role in mitophagy functions through Mfn2.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C102 are supported by data showing p97 requirement for complex disassembly (Figure 5E-G) and mtKeima experiments (Figure 7A-B) showing that p97 inhibition doesn't block mitophagy in Mfn2-depleted cells. This establishes epistasis between p97 and Mfn2.

results.result: p97 relieves Mfn2-dependent inhibition of VDAC1 ubiquitination, as VDAC1 ubiquitination is sensitive to p97 inhibition in control cells but not Mfn2-depleted cells, with the half-time of VDAC1 modification increasing two-fold with NMS-873 specifically in control cells, demonstrating that Mfn2 gates the availability of the stable parkin receptor VDAC1.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C107 are supported by time-course immunoblots (Figure 7C-H) showing differential effects of p97 inhibition on VDAC1 ubiquitination in control vs Mfn2-depleted cells. This provides a mechanistic explanation for how Mfn2 removal facilitates mitophagy.

results.result: Parkin-dependent ubiquitination of Mfn2 can be reconstituted on isolated mitochondria in a time-, depolarization-, ligase-, and PINK1-dependent manner, with cytosolic mouse parkin able to catalyze Mfn2 ubiquitination, and co-incubation with cytosol enabling robust ubiquitination of both Mfn2 and VDAC1.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 are supported by in organello ubiquitination assays (Figure 8C-I) showing reconstitution of the system with appropriate controls. This demonstrates that the key components are sufficient to recapitulate the cellular observations.

results.result: In cytosol-containing reactions, VDAC1 ubiquitination displays sensitivity to NMS-873, and addition of recombinant p97 hexamer stimulates both Mfn2 and VDAC1 ubiquitination in a parkin-dependent manner, with p97 enabling Mfn2 retrotranslocation, demonstrating reconstitution of PINK1/parkin-dependent, p97-stimulated Mfn2 and VDAC1 ubiquitination and Mfn2 retrotranslocation in a cell-free assay.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C118 are supported by in organello experiments with cytosol and recombinant p97 (Figure 8J-N) showing p97-dependent stimulation of ubiquitination and Mfn2 retrotranslocation. This provides strong biochemical evidence for the proposed mechanism.

results.result: PINK1, parkin and p97 collaborate to uncouple OMM-ER contacts via Mfn2 ubiquitination and degradation during mitophagy, which in turn allows ubiquitination and degradation of additional parkin substrates such as VDAC1.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C120 represent the central mechanistic conclusion of the paper, supported by the convergence of cellular and in organello experiments. The model is well-supported by the data showing sequential events: Mfn2 ubiquitination → p97-mediated extraction → ER-OMM uncoupling → enhanced VDAC1 ubiquitination.

results.result: There is a requirement for parkin, PINK1, p97 and proteasomal activity in the destruction of mitochondria-ER contacts during mitophagy.
results.evaluation: Claim C122 is supported by experiments using PINK1 depletion, parkin mutants, p97 inhibition, and proteasome inhibition (Figure 1H-J, Figure 5F-H, Figure 6). This establishes the complete set of factors required for contact site destruction.

results.result: Mfn2 is rapidly phosphoubiquitinated upon mitophagy induction, Mfn2-containing HMW complexes are extracted by p97 requiring HR1 domain ubiquitination, and both reduction of Mfn2 ubiquitination and p97 inhibition repress mitophagy, with the main concepts reconstitutable in a cell-free assay.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C128 summarize key findings supported by multiple experiments throughout the paper. This represents the core mechanistic discovery linking Mfn2 phosphoubiquitination, p97-mediated extraction, and mitophagy regulation.

results.result: The PINK1/parkin/p97 axis acts rapidly on Mfn2 HMW complexes to separate mitochondria from the ER to facilitate mitophagy, potentially by making more substrates available, with the intriguing possibility that mitochondria-ER contacts are initial sites of PINK1/parkin activity and Ub phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C130 represent the proposed model (Figure 9) based on the experimental findings. C129 is well-supported by the data, while C130 is more speculative but reasonable given the rapid Mfn2 ubiquitination at contact sites.

results.result: Mfn2 bridges between mitochondria and ER may form ring-like structures similar to yeast Fzo1p, potentially restricting substrate availability to parkin/PINK1, with PINK1 localizing to the MAM upon depolarization and VDACs physically interacting with ER IP3 receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C134 are largely speculative (C132) or based on prior work (C131, C133-C134). While the structural model is plausible and consistent with the data, direct evidence for ring formation by Mfn2 at ER-OMM contacts is not provided in this study.

results.result: The existence of a ~500 kDa Mfn2-containing interorganellar bridge is supported by BN-PAGE data showing Mfn2 uniquely exists as a homotypic dimer of ~250 kDa subunits, correlating with reduced Mfn2 GTPase activity compared to Mfn1, with complex stability negatively regulated by parkin-mediated ubiquitination coupled to p97-dependent retrotranslocation.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C137 are supported by BN-PAGE data (Figure 5A) and citations to prior structural work. The interpretation is consistent with known mitofusin biology and the experimental observations of complex disassembly.

results.result: Both ubiquitinated and unmodified forms of retrotranslocated Mfn2 are observed upon p97 addition, suggesting that while the hexamer may engage directly with Mfn2 at high concentrations, Ub-binding cofactors may localize p97 to ubiquitinated Mfn2 at physiological levels, consistent with p97 recognizing both Ub-dependent and intrinsic signals in ERAD.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C140 are supported by fractionation data (Figure 8N) and citation to Ye et al., 2003. The speculation about cofactor involvement (C139) is reasonable given the observation of both modified and unmodified retrotranslocated Mfn2.

results.result: MITOL-mediated Mfn2 ubiquitination on different lysine residues can positively regulate complex formation and mitochondria-ER tethering, emphasizing Mfn2 ubiquitination as an important regulator of mitochondria-ER contact.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C142 integrate prior work (Sugiura et al., 2013) with current findings to emphasize that different ubiquitination patterns on Mfn2 can have opposite effects. This is well-supported and provides important context.

results.result: Robust parkin activation during mitophagy occurs through a feed-forward mechanism involving PINK1-phosphorylated Ub, with the Mfns undergoing a burst of phosphoubiquitination at mitophagy onset driven by localized parkin activation, showing preference for Mfns above other substrates like HK1 and Miro1, followed by rapid p97-mediated extraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C147 integrate prior mechanistic understanding with current findings about substrate hierarchy. The data clearly show temporal preference for Mfn ubiquitination (Figures 2A-C, 8F) and rapid extraction (Figures 5A, 5E, 8N).

results.result: It is unlikely that Mfn1 or Mfn2 act as parkin receptors during mitophagy given their rapid turnover and enhanced parkin recruitment in Mfn2-deficient cells, with Mfn2 acting as a stable parkin tether only when p97 retrotranslocation is inhibited, while VDAC1 is involved in a stable complex tethering parkin to the OMM.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C150 are supported by rapid Mfn turnover data, enhanced recruitment in Mfn2-deficient cells (Figure 3C-E), stabilization with p97 inhibition (Figure 6J-K), and citation to Callegari et al., 2017 for VDAC1. This clarifies the receptor vs substrate distinction.

results.result: Mfn2 may act as a parkin receptor in cardiomyocytes where mitophagy plays a role in metabolic development rather than quality control, with phosphorylation of Mfn2 on T111 and S442 by a cardiac-specific kinase potentially facilitating mitophagy by uncoupling mitochondria from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C152 are largely speculative, attempting to reconcile tissue-specific differences in Mfn2 function. While supported by citations and the observation that Mfn2T111A/S442A blocks mitophagy in heart but not cell lines, direct evidence for the proposed mechanism is lacking.

results.result: Mitophagy functions as a quality control mechanism while starvation-induced autophagy is a metabolic response, with starvation-induced autophagy initiation at mitochondria-ER contact sites potentially serving to decode metabolic needs, and mitochondrial damage potentially precluding mitochondria from serving as an autophagosomal membrane source during mitophagy.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C157 discuss fundamental differences between mitophagy and starvation-induced autophagy. C153-C154 are well-established, C155 is reasonable speculation, C156 is supported by citations, and C157 is logical speculation about why damaged mitochondria wouldn't serve as membrane sources.

results.result: The SNARE Stx17 governs autophagosome-lysosome fusion during starvation but is dispensable for mitophagy, instead appearing to suppress mitophagy through its role in supporting mitochondria-ER contact.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C160 are supported by citations (Itakura et al., 2012b; McLelland et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2016; Arasaki et al., 2015) and data (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G-I). This highlights another difference between mitophagy and starvation-induced autophagy.

results.result: Mitophagy shares morphological and several mechanistic similarities with canonical macroautophagy, including recruitment of ULK1 complexes and ATG9A vesicles to depolarized mitochondria.
results.evaluation: Claim C161 is supported by citations (Itakura et al., 2012a; Lazarou et al., 2015) and acknowledges that despite differences, mitophagy shares some features with canonical autophagy. This provides balanced context.

results.result: In Drosophila, phenotypes of PINK1 and PRKN mutants are duplicated by MARF overexpression and suppressed by p97 overexpression, with PINK1/parkin/p97 counteracting MARF through its ubiquitination and turnover in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C164 are supported by citations to fly studies (Yun et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2016; Ziviani et al., 2010). This provides important in vivo validation of the mechanism in a model organism.

results.result: A proposed mechanism of cell death due to PINK1 deletion is sensitization of mitochondria to Ca2+ overload, with deletion of the mitochondrial Ca2+ uniporter protecting dopaminergic neurons from cell death in PINK1-deficient zebrafish.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C166 are supported by citations (Akundi et al., 2011; Gandhi et al., 2009; Kostic et al., 2015; Soman et al., 2017). This provides disease-relevant context suggesting dysregulated mitochondria-ER contact may contribute to pathology.

results.result: An increased degree of mitochondria-ER contact has been observed in fibroblasts from PRKN and PINK1 patients and brains from mutant flies, while transient PINK1 depletion destabilizes mitochondria-ER tethering.
results.evaluation: Claims C167-C168 acknowledge conflicting observations in the literature regarding steady-state ER-OMM contacts in PINK1/parkin loss-of-function models. The authors appropriately note differences in quantification methods and experimental conditions.
